Tidal power turns the regular rise and fall of the sea into electricity. The moon and the sun pull on the oceans, and where a narrow bay or estuary funnels the water, the difference between high and low tide can reach many metres. A power station built across such a bay can capture that difference twice a day, in every season, on a timetable that engineers can publish years ahead. The oldest design is the barrage, a low dam with gates and turbines set into it. At high tide the gates open and the bay fills; at low tide the water is released through the turbines and the generators spin. The Rance station in Brittany, which opened in 1966, uses twenty-four turbines and still supplies several hundred gigawatt-hours every year. Its builders also had to manage the silt, the salt and the fish that pass through the estuary. A barrage changes the bay behind it. Mudflats that were covered and uncovered twice a day may stay wetter or drier than before, wading birds lose feeding grounds, and the flow of sediment shifts. Environmental reviews of later proposals therefore weigh the energy gained against the habitat altered, and several large schemes have been shelved because the estimated damage outweighed the benefit. Tidal stream turbines work differently. Instead of a dam, they stand in the open current like underwater wind turbines, and the moving water turns the blades. Because water is about eight hundred times denser than air, a slow current carries a great deal of energy, and the machines can be much smaller than a wind turbine of the same output. The MeyGen array in the Pentland Firth, off the north coast of Scotland, has delivered power to the grid since 2017. Cost remains the main obstacle. Marine equipment must survive corrosion, storms and the strong currents that make a site attractive in the first place, and every maintenance visit needs a vessel and a calm window. Early projects have been expensive per unit of electricity, although the price has fallen as designs have been standardised and the first arrays have gathered operating data. Supporters point to predictability. Wind and sunshine vary with the weather, but the tide table is known long in advance, so operators and grid managers can plan around it. Tides in different places peak at different hours, so a handful of sites spread along a coast could together provide a steadier supply than any one of them alone. Researchers are also studying tidal lagoons, which enclose a stretch of shoreline with a sea wall and generate power as the water flows in and out of the pool. Supporters say a lagoon disturbs less of the open estuary than a full barrage, while critics note that the walls are long, costly and still change the local habitat. Several pilot plans remain under discussion in Britain, China and South Korea.

Geothermal energy taps the heat stored beneath the surface of the Earth. In some regions hot rock lies close enough to the surface that wells a few kilometres deep reach water at two hundred degrees or more, and the steam or hot water that rises can drive a turbine or warm the buildings of an entire town. Iceland is the best known example. Volcanic activity under the island heats the groundwater, and nearly every home in Reykjavik is warmed by water piped from nearby fields. The same fields supply a large share of the country's electricity, which is why heavy industry such as aluminium smelting has settled there. A conventional plant needs three things at once: heat, water and permeable rock. Where one is missing, engineers sometimes build an enhanced system, drilling two wells into hot dry rock and fracturing the space between them so that injected water can circulate, pick up heat and return to the surface. The method opens many more sites, but it has also caused small earthquakes near some projects, and operators now monitor the ground closely. Compared with wind and solar power, geothermal plants run day and night in any weather, so they can supply the steady base load that a grid needs. Their fuel costs nothing, although drilling is expensive and a poorly placed well can dry up. Operators reinject the used water to keep the reservoir full, which also limits the release of dissolved gases. Smaller systems exist too. A heat pump buried in the garden of a house moves warmth from the ground into the building in winter and reverses the flow in summer, using far less electricity than a furnace or a conventional air conditioner. Millions of such installations now operate in Sweden, the United States and China. The main limits are geography and cost. The richest fields lie along plate boundaries, far from many large cities, and an exploratory well can cost as much as a small factory before anyone knows whether it will produce. Public loan guarantees and shared drilling data have helped several countries bring new fields into service.

L'énergie marémotrice transforme le va-et-vient des marées en électricité : c'est la plus régulière des énergies de la mer. La Lune et le Soleil attirent les océans, et dans un estuaire étroit la différence entre la haute et la basse mer peut dépasser douze mètres. L'usine de la Rance, en Bretagne, a été mise en service en 1966. Elle compte vingt-quatre turbines et produit chaque année environ cinq cent soixante gigawattheures ; ses ingénieurs ont dû résoudre des problèmes de corrosion, de sable et de poissons migrateurs, puis surveiller pendant des décennies l'évolution de la vasière située en amont. Les hydroliennes fonctionnent autrement : elles sont posées dans le courant, comme des éoliennes sous l'eau. L'eau étant environ huit cents fois plus dense que l'air, un courant lent suffit pour entraîner des pales bien plus petites. Les premiers parcs, en Écosse et au Raz Blanchard, livrent déjà de l'électricité au réseau. Reste la question du coût : l'équipement marin doit résister à la tempête, au sel et aux courants violents, et chaque intervention exige un navire et une fenêtre météo favorable. Les partisans répondent que la prévisibilité des marées facilite la gestion du réseau ; les écologistes demandent quant à eux que les projets soient jugés sur leur effet réel sur les oiseaux, les poissons et les sédiments.

attestation.text: Tidal power turns the regular rise and fall of the sea into electricity. The moon and the sun pull on the oceans, and where a narrow bay or estuary funnels the water, the difference between high and low tide can reach many metres. anchor.title: Marées et énergie
anchor.text: L'énergie marémotrice transforme le va-et-vient des marées en électricité : c'est la plus régulière des énergies de la mer. La Lune et le Soleil attirent les océans, et dans un estuaire étroit la différence entre la haute et la basse mer peut dépasser douze mètres. Publicité : assurance bateau, jusqu'à trente pour cent d'économie. L'usine de la Rance, en Bretagne, a été mise en service en 1966. Elle compte vingt-quatre turbines et produit chaque année environ cinq cent soixante gigawattheures ; ses ingénieurs ont dû résoudre des problèmes de corrosion, de sable et de poissons migrateurs, puis surveiller pendant des décennies l'évolution de la vasière située en amont. Les hydroliennes fonctionnent autrement : elles sont posées dans le courant, comme des éoliennes sous l'eau. L'eau étant environ huit cents fois plus dense que l'air, un courant lent suffit pour entraîner des pales bien plus petites. Les premiers parcs, en Écosse et au Raz Blanchard, livrent déjà de l'électricité au réseau. Reste la question du coût : l'équipement marin doit résister à la tempête, au sel et aux courants violents, et chaque intervention exige un navire et une fenêtre météo favorable. Les partisans répondent que la prévisibilité des marées facilite la gestion du réseau ; les écologistes demandent quant à eux que les projets soient jugés sur leur effet réel sur les oiseaux, les poissons et les sédiments. Mis à jour le 14 octobre 2026 à 09 h 12.

attestation.title: Geothermal energy
attestation.text: Geothermal energy taps the heat stored beneath the surface of the Earth. In some regions hot rock lies close enough to the surface that wells a few kilometres deep reach water at two hundred degrees or more, and the steam or hot water that rises can drive a turbine or warm the buildings of an entire town. Iceland is the best known example. Volcanic activity under the island heats the groundwater, and nearly every home in Reykjavik is warmed by water piped from nearby fields. The same fields supply a large share of the country's electricity, which is why heavy industry such as aluminium smelting has settled there. A conventional plant needs three things at once: heat, water and permeable rock. Where one is missing, engineers sometimes build an enhanced system, drilling two wells into hot dry rock and fracturing the space between them so that injected water can circulate, pick up heat and return to the surface. The method opens many more sites, but it has also caused small earthquakes near some projects, and operators now monitor the ground closely. Compared with wind and solar power, geothermal plants run day and night in any weather, so they can supply the steady base load that a grid needs. Their fuel costs nothing, although drilling is expensive and a poorly placed well can dry up. Operators reinject the used water to keep the reservoir full, which also limits the release of dissolved gases. Smaller systems exist too. A heat pump buried in the garden of a house moves warmth from the ground into the building in winter and reverses the flow in summer, using far less electricity than a furnace or a conventional air conditioner. Millions of such installations now operate in Sweden, the United States and China. The main limits are geography and cost. The richest fields lie along plate boundaries, far from many large cities, and an exploratory well can cost as much as a small factory before anyone knows whether it will produce. Public loan guarantees and shared drilling data have helped several countries bring new fields into service.
